source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina, Gray (2009) Do New Caledonian crows solve physical problems through causal reasoning? Proc R Soc B 276:247-254
finding: Founding design: a two-trap tube, then step-by-step removal of arbitrary cues (triangulation, Heyes 1993), then a visually different trap-table. Only a causal-feature account survives the whole series. Authors conclude causal reasoning is a component of crow cognition.
numbers: 6 wild crows from Mare (5 adult, 1 sub-adult; 2 female), tested Jan-Mar 2008. Initial tube had 3 arbitrary cues: yellow disc at trap base, yellow disc at non-functional mouth, blue rim. Solve criterion 17/20 over two 10-trial blocks (alpha .01); stop at 150 trials. Transfer criterion 15/20 (alpha .05).
quote: The most compelling way to eliminate the possibility of associative learning is to present an animal with a visually distinct but causally equivalent task.
limits: Tiny N, wild-caught birds, one lab. Credit needs both cue-free transfer and a control for generalisation.
agent_relevance: S4/G3: a pass counts only after the cues the answer could have been fitted to are removed one at a time, and then a new surface form is used.

source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina, Gray (2009) Do New Caledonian crows solve physical problems through causal reasoning? Proc R Soc B 276:247-254
finding: Learning phase: only half the crows learned the initial trap-tube, and slowly. Successful crows switched probing side in 22.1% of trials, unsuccessful crows in 0%. Authors suggest inhibitory control matters.
numbers: 3 of 6 crows (Obo, Tiga, Slevin) solved in under 150 trials; mean 103.3 +/- 20.3 trials. 91.2% +/- 2.7 of trials were pulls, not pushes. Side switching 22.1 +/- 9.0% vs 0%: U=9, p=0.0318 one-tailed. Inspection 22.0 vs 13.7% (p=0.5); trap probing 3.1 vs 1.3% (p=0.5). Espanol halted pulling at the trap edge in 16.6% of trials but never switched side.
limits: Mann-Whitney on 3 vs 3 birds has very low power. The inhibition story is post hoc.
agent_relevance: A 50% solve rate after 100+ trials means the transfer result is conditional on a slow, noisy training stage. A pass is not typical.

source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina, Gray (2009) Do New Caledonian crows solve physical problems through causal reasoning? Proc R Soc B 276:247-254
finding: Transfer 1 (yellow discs removed, blue rim kept) and Transfer 2 (discs black, blue rim removed) were both solved by all three crows. So no single arbitrary cue was needed.
numbers: Transfers 1 and 2: 3 of 3 crows above chance (15/20 criterion). First trials pooled over all four transfers: trap avoided in 10 of 12.
limits: First-trial success did not predict later success: Tiga pulled into the trap on trial 1 of transfer 2, then avoided it in the next 19 trials.
agent_relevance: A lucky first answer is not evidence either way; judge the block, not the first sample.

source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina, Gray (2009) Do New Caledonian crows solve physical problems through causal reasoning? Proc R Soc B 276:247-254
finding: Transfer 3 (one functional trap with a base, one bottomless hole): all three crows FAILED. They had learned 'avoid the hole', not 'avoid the trap base'. Crows often shuffled the meat between the holes without pulling it into either.
numbers: 3 of 3 failed. Latency to finish and side switching were highest in transfer 3 for all three crows; chance of that pattern p=0.0156 (binomial, n=3, p0=0.25). Tiga and Slevin avoided the trap on trial 1, then performed at chance for 19 trials.
quote: If the crows were capable of more sophisticated causal reasoning, they would have viewed the meat's relations with the hole and the trap base as two separate proximate causal regularities.
limits: Key boundary: transfer reached a new look but not a new causal feature. Authors read it as a proximate regularity, not an inferred distal mechanism (gravity).
agent_relevance: A pass on a re-skinned task does not show the deeper rule was learned. Add a test where the old surface cue and the true cause point in different directions.

source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina, Gray (2009) Do New Caledonian crows solve physical problems through causal reasoning? Proc R Soc B 276:247-254
finding: Transfer 4, the trap-table, differs from the tube in shape, colour and material. All three successful crows were correct on trial 1 and solved it quickly. The three crows that failed the tube also failed the table, which rules out a general hole-avoidance disposition.
numbers: 3 of 3 successful crows solved the trap-table at first trial and rapidly (15/20 criterion). 3 of 3 non-learners failed the table. Table 10x15x6 cm, rectangular trap 5x3 cm, rake dowel 15 cm. In 10 of 12 first transfer trials neither trap nor surface was probed.
limits: Rival accounts considered and rejected by the authors: chance, visual and tactile generalisation (Shepard 1987), prior disposition. Spatial-analogy and sampling-error objections were answered in a short 2009 follow-up in Commun Integr Biol (not opened).
agent_relevance: Strongest 'not fitted to' evidence in the series: success on a task sharing no surface features. But 3 animals, long training.

source: Taylor (2020) Folk physics for crows? Animal Behavior and Cognition 7(3):452-456
finding: The first author reviews the crow work 11 years later. The trap-tube pass shows causal knowledge of observable features (hole, surface) but not of an unobservable mechanism (gravity). Povinelli's thesis for apes also fits crows. He still warns against a final negative.
numbers: Recaps: 3 of 6 crows learned the tube; four transfers; failure on the two-hole transfer; Neilands et al. 2016 found no preference for heavy over light stones (weight inattention error).
quote: Clearly, at present, there does not seem to be any evidence that NC crows reason about unobservable causal mechanisms.
limits: Argues tests jump in difficulty. Proposes a ladder in one paradigm: hidden object, then hidden agent or mechanism, then unobservable cause. Performance depends on task format (pull vs push, Mulcahy and Call 2006).
agent_relevance: Same design advice for us: climb inference difficulty in small steps within one paradigm, so a failure can be located.

source: Martin-Ordas, Call, Colmenares (2008) Tubes, tables and traps: great apes solve two functionally equivalent trap tasks but show no evidence of transfer across tasks. Anim Cogn 11:423-430
finding: The direct ape comparison: apes learn both a trap-tube (push or rake allowed) and a trap-platform, but performance on one does not predict performance on the other. It is the contrast case the crow paper sets itself against.
numbers: 20 apes (gorilla, chimpanzee, bonobo, orangutan), 3 sessions of 12 trials per task (72 total). 12/20 solved the platform, 8/20 the tube. 5 solved both, 7 platform only, 3 tube only, 5 neither. Cross-task correlation r=0.13, p=0.57, n=20. Platform better than tube F(1,16)=3.46, p=0.04 one-tailed. First trial correct: platform 14/20 (p=0.074), tube 12/20 (p=0.37).
limits: No species differences, but small sample. Authors offer two readings: knowledge tied to actions, or no causal knowledge. Apes preferred raking over pushing (z=1.98, p=0.024). Previous trap experience did not help.
agent_relevance: Zero cross-task correlation on matched structure is the pattern expected from surface-fitted solvers; usable as a test.

source: Silva, Page, Silva (2005) Methodological-conceptual problems in the study of chimpanzees' folk physics: how studies with adult humans can help. Learn Behav 33:47-58
finding: Adult humans fail the inverted-trap control: they still avoid a non-functional trap and insert the tool at the end far from the reward. So 'avoids the inverted trap' cannot be read as lack of understanding. This undermines the classic ape control.
numbers: Exp 1: 10 undergraduates, 15 configurations. Far end, no trap or ineffective trap: 52/60 (p<.001). Reward equidistant: 16/30 right end (p=.856). Effective trap: 40/40 far end; trap nearest: 10/10. Ineffective-trap configurations c-f: 36/40 far end. Context: chimp Megan used the far end on 39/40 inverted-trap trials. Three experiments in total.
limits: Humans had verbal instruction and opaque tubes. Exp 2 used symbolic diagrams and replicated most of Exp 1.
agent_relevance: A control that even a competent agent fails is a bad control. Check that our own G3 checks pass for a known-good solver.

source: Voelter and Call (2014) The cognitive underpinnings of flexible tool use in great apes. J Exp Psychol Anim Learn Cogn
finding: Apes fail trap tasks largely because of tool-use load. A maze solved with fingers beat the same maze with a stick, and tool users did no better than apes who saw only arbitrary colour cues. Experienced apes later generalised trap knowledge to colour cues but did not plan with them.
numbers: Chimpanzees, bonobos and orangutans (14 chimpanzees in the sample). Finger-maze apes outperformed tool-maze apes. Intro cites Mulcahy and Call 2006: 3 of 8 apes solved the raking tube in 24 to 60 trials and passed the inverted control.
quote: Nonhuman primates perform poorly in trap tasks, a benchmark test of causal knowledge in nonhuman animals.
limits: Explains the Martin-Ordas null: the cost of monitoring two spatial relations can mask causal knowledge.
agent_relevance: A fail can come from interface cost, not missing understanding. Lower the interface cost before concluding an agent cannot reason.

source: Jelbert, Taylor, Cheke, Clayton, Gray (2014) Using the Aesop's fable paradigm to investigate causal understanding of water displacement by New Caledonian crows. PLoS ONE 9:e92895
finding: Same lab, new causal domain, a battery of six tasks of graded difficulty. Crows pass the intuitive ones and fail the tube-width task and the counter-intuitive U-tube. Verdict: sophisticated but incomplete causal understanding, like 5 to 7 year old children.
numbers: 6 crows. Exp 1: 76.3% of drops into water vs sand over 20 trials (p=0.001); 5 of 6 individually significant within 15 trials. Sinking vs floating, solid vs hollow, high vs low water also passed. Failed: narrow vs wide (narrow first on 56% of trials, p=0.27) and the U-tube. Intro cites trap-tube pass rates: 2 of 5 chimpanzees over 140 trials, 3 of 6 NC crows over 150 trials, 7 of 8 rooks over 150 trials.
limits: The analysis is the pattern of passes and fails over a graded battery. A later skeptical analysis (not opened) says subjects may learn from successful actions only.
agent_relevance: A graded battery with deliberately hard items is a template for telling whether a scaffold understands or pattern-matches.

source: Seed, Tebbich, Emery, Clayton (2006) Investigating physical cognition in rooks, Corvus frugilegus. Curr Biol 16:697-701
finding: Prior work the crow study builds on: the two-trap tube in rooks, with transfers that reversed the response required by familiar arbitrary features. One rook may have used surface continuity and solidity. Not opened (paywall); reported via Taylor 2009 and Jelbert 2014.
numbers: 7 of 8 rooks passed in 150 trials (Jelbert 2014 intro). One rook passed the transfers (Taylor 2009). A web summary also says seven of eight solved the initial task.
limits: The rook was not given a functionally equivalent second task (Taylor 2009 point). A web snippet says Tebbich et al. 2007 had 3 of 7 rooks solve a modified problem.
agent_relevance: Reversing the response the old cue demands is a sharper test than removing the cue. Consider it for G3.

source: Visalberghi and Limongelli (1994) Lack of comprehension of cause-effect relations in tool-using capuchin monkeys. J Comp Psychol 108:15-22
finding: Original trap-tube: capuchins that learned to push food out did not change when the tube was inverted, read as associative learning. Not opened; described in Taylor 2009, Silva 2005, Voelter and Call 2014.
numbers: Per Voelter and Call 2014: the one successful capuchin only learned to insert the tool farthest from the reward. Per Silva 2005: only 3 of 9 chimpanzees (pooled Limongelli 1995 and Reaux and Povinelli 2000) reached above-chance.
limits: Push-only apparatus later shown to confound results (Mulcahy and Call 2006).
agent_relevance: Birth of the inverted-trap control, later shown flawed. Do not copy it unchanged into G3 checks.

source: Girndt, Meier, Call (2008) and Mulcahy and Call (2006), as reported in Taylor 2009 and Voelter and Call 2014
finding: Apes do better when tool constraints are lifted: 20 of 24 apes avoided the trap on trial 1 with one tool on the trap-table (Girndt 2008); with a raking option 3 of 8 apes solved the tube and passed the inverted control (Mulcahy and Call 2006). Originals not opened.
numbers: 20/24 first-trial trap avoidance (Girndt 2008, per Taylor 2009); 3/8 solved in 24 to 60 trials (Mulcahy and Call 2006, per Voelter and Call 2014).
limits: Girndt did not test a prior disposition to avoid holes (Taylor 2009).
agent_relevance: Design flaws, not species, can explain many failures. Same caution applies to LLM evals.

source: Povinelli (2000) Folk Physics for Apes, thesis as restated in Taylor 2020 and Silva 2005
finding: Reinterpretation hypothesis: apes learn regularities between events but do not invoke unobservable causes such as force or gravity. This is the theory the trap tasks test. Book not opened; quote from Taylor 2020.
numbers: 27 experiments by Povinelli and collaborators (Silva 2005). Chimp Megan solved the tube, then used the far end on 39/40 inverted-trap trials; solved the trap-table within 20 trials, though earlier trap-table training may have taught a surface rule (Taylor 2009).
quote: chimpanzees detect the regularities that exist between events ... but they do not appeal to unobservable phenomena
limits: Rival views: causal reasoning is analogical, tied to actions (Martin-Ordas), or cost-limited (Voelter and Call).
agent_relevance: Frames the exact question for an LLM: regularity learning on the surface vs inference of a hidden cause.

source: Farrar et al. (2020) Trialling meta-research in comparative cognition: claims and statistical inference in animal physical cognition. Anim Behav Cogn 7(3):419-444
finding: Meta-research on 116 experiments from 63 papers, 14 of them trap-tube variants. Samples are tiny, results often rest on a few passers, and a p-value dip just above .05 hints at publication bias. Applies to the crow result too.
numbers: 116 experiments, 63 papers, 1994-2019, 45 species. Median N=7 animals. Of 87 experiments with a pass count, 15 had zero animals pass and 25 had all pass; median share passing 0.6; median passers 3 (max 17). Positive claims 44-59%, inconclusive 24-46%, negative 10-17%. 40 experiments used both group and individual tests, 28 group only, 48 individual only.
limits: Keyword sampling over-represents trap-tube and tool-use studies. No formal p-curve possible. Authors say exact numbers may not represent the field.
agent_relevance: Treat 3-of-6 passes as hypothesis-generating. For us: report pass counts out of N attempts, never a single run.

source: Voudouris, Crosby, Beyret, Hernandez-Orallo, Shanahan, Halina, Cheke (2022) Direct human-AI comparison in the Animal-AI environment. Front Psychol 13:711821
finding: First direct comparison of children and AI agents on animal-cognition-style tasks (Animal-AI Testbed, 10 levels including avoidance, causal reasoning and tool use). Children beat 30 competition agents on almost every level.
numbers: 52 children aged 6-10 vs 30 AI agents, 40 tasks (4 per level). Children median 0.6276, mean 0.6052 (SD 0.1476); AIs median 0.3529, mean 0.3412 (SD 0.0809). On average 0% of AIs passed Levels 3, 6, 8, 9 and 10 (causal reasoning). No significant child-AI difference on L1 or L2; all other levels differed significantly with large effects.
limits: Children tested online without an experimenter; agents trained on the environment, not these tasks. Best agents 'ironbar' and 'Trrrrr' still differed significantly from children (Hotelling T2).
agent_relevance: The AI side of the paradigm: trained agents break down when the layout changes.

source: Mecattaf, Slater, Voudouris, Tesic, Prunty, Cheke (2024) A little less conversation, a little more action, please: investigating the physical common-sense of LLMs in a 3D embodied environment. arXiv 2410.23242
finding: First LLM test in the Animal-AI Testbed. Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro (multimodal, no fine-tuning) controlled an agent. They cleared easy navigation levels but did worse than children on every level and never beat the top-10 Olympics agents.
numbers: 3 models, temperature 0, 3 trials each on 40 tasks (4 per level, 12 trials per level); child baseline 59 children aged 6-10 (Voudouris 2022 data). LLMs completed some L1 and L2 tasks, sporadic L5, L6, L8; comparable to competition agents only in L3, L8, L9, L10 at very low rates (floor effect). An in-context 'expert example' made no notable difference; GPT's L3 rate rose to the upper quartile of competition agents.
quote: The children perform convincingly better than the LLM agents across all levels
limits: One image per turn; coarse controls; convenience sample of three models; results given as plots and rates.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM test of animal-style physical causal transfer. Frontier models are still weak when the answer needs acting in a new layout.

source: Voudouris, Cheke, Schulz (2025) Bringing comparative cognition to computers. arXiv 2503.02882
finding: Position paper: AI psychology should adopt comparative cognition methods to avoid both under- and over-attribution (Clever Hans, dogs and object permanence). Warns LLM failure on large-number arithmetic may be test design, not missing capacity.
numbers: Qualitative. No new experiment.
limits: Position piece, not an empirical test.
agent_relevance: Backs G3: check a pass against Clever Hans explanations, and a fail against task-design artefacts.

source: Rane, Kirkman, Todd, Royka, Law, Cartmill, Foster (2025) Position: principles of animal cognition to improve LLM evaluations. ICML, PMLR 267:82051-82061
finding: Five principles from animal cognition, tested on transitive inference in GPT-4o. Same logic as a trap-tube transfer: strip the surface cue and see if the pass survives. It did not.
numbers: Accuracy fell as transitive elements and ordinal operators were removed: A vs C 1.00; B vs D 1.00; ranked animals 0.97; random strings 0.92; reverse-ranked 0.78; n-term trial-based 0.40 (S.D. 0.50). After 60 training trials on adjacent pairs, novel non-adjacent pairs were answered at chance, with no symbolic-distance effect.
quote: performance dropped significantly after the introduction of control conditions that abstracted the task
limits: One model (GPT-4o), one capacity; the five principles are argued, not measured.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue of the crow transfer logic: a pass on familiar wording can hide a failure on the same structure in new form. Reuse the stripping ladder.

source: Jin et al. (2023) CLadder: assessing causal reasoning in language models. NeurIPS; arXiv 2312.04350
finding: About 10K causal questions across Pearl's ladder, in commonsensical, anti-commonsensical and nonsensical story versions as a check against memorised content. Most models sit near chance; GPT-4 with a causal chain-of-thought prompt reaches 70.4%.
numbers: Overall accuracy: random 49.27; LLaMa 44.03; Alpaca 44.66; GPT-3 davinci 49.92; text-davinci-003 56.26; GPT-3.5 52.18; GPT-4 62.03; GPT-4 + CausalCoT 70.40. CausalCoT by rung: 83.35, 67.47, 62.05. Plain GPT-4 was 1.8 points worse on anti-commonsensical than commonsensical; CausalCoT gained 9.65 points on anti-commonsensical.
limits: Formal Pearl-style questions, not physical tasks. Yes or no answers, so chance is 50%. v1.5 balanced set has 10,112 questions.
agent_relevance: Same surface-swap logic as the crow work: change the story, keep the structure. A prompt that adds explicit structure helps.

source: Choudhary et al. (2025) Stochastic parrot see, stochastic parrot do. Cognitive Science Society proceedings
finding: Compares hierarchical reasoning in 4 LLM generations with adults, children, crows and monkeys; reports it appears across generations on a continuum with the biological groups, strongest in newer reasoning models. Only an abstract snippet via search; page blocked.
numbers: 4 LLM generations vs 4 biological groups (search summary only).
limits: Not opened; details unverified.
agent_relevance: One of few LLM papers placing crows beside models. Read in full before use.

source: Taylor et al. (2014, 2015) Of babies and birds; No conclusive evidence that corvids can create novel causal interventions. Proc R Soc B 281:20140837, 282:20150796
finding: Same lab's later causal-intervention test with crows and young children: crows did not create novel causal interventions. Known from titles and Taylor 2020 reference list; paper not opened.
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Titles alone; findings unverified.
agent_relevance: Suggests strong causal claims shrink under stricter intervention tests.

source: Blaisdell, Sawa, Leising, Waldmann (2006) Causal reasoning in rats. Science 311:1020-1022
finding: Cited in Taylor 2009 as evidence animals are sensitive to causal structure. OpenAlex lists reappraisals ('Causal reasoning in rats: a reappraisal', 2009; 'The special status of actions in causal reasoning in rats', 2008) with associative accounts. Not opened.
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Only titles seen.
agent_relevance: Same pattern: a causal headline, then an associative rival.

source: Voudouris et al. (2023) The Animal-AI Environment: a virtual laboratory for comparative cognition and AI research. arXiv 2312.11414
finding: Describes the Animal-AI Testbed (10 levels, 30 tasks x 3 variants = 900 tasks) and tests PPO and Dreamer-v3. Causal Reasoning, Object Permanence and Working Memory, and Numerosity levels are hard for all agents, children included.
numbers: 900 tasks across 10 levels. Dreamer-v3 would have placed 25th in the 2019 competition (from search summary; text partly read).
quote: Three levels ... pose difficulty for all agents, including children
limits: Dreamer-v3 placement unverified in the text; partial read.
agent_relevance: A reusable physical-causal transfer testbed for embodied evaluation.

source: Aesop's fable critique (skeptical analysis surfaced by search; see Jelbert 2014 PMC3966847)
finding: Search summary only: a skeptical analysis says Aesop's fable results may come from learning from successful actions, so trial-and-error cannot be told from causal reasoning. Not opened.
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Unverified.
agent_relevance: A pattern of passes may reflect success-driven learning, not rules.
